claim: C. elegans body muscles receive direct inhibitory input from GABAergic motor neurons
source: C. elegans body muscles receive direct inhibitory input from GABAergic motor neurons (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 1986

claim: The GABAA receptors found at C. elegans neuromuscular junctions contain two subunits (UNC-49B and C) both encoded by the unc-49 gene
source: The GABAA receptors found at these NMJs contain two subunits (UNC-49B and C) both encoded by the unc-49 gene (Bamber et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bamber et al., 1999

claim: Mutants lacking UNC-49 receptors have defects in GABA-activated muscle currents
source: Mutants lacking UNC-49 receptors have defects in GABA-activated muscle currents, as assessed by recording miniature inhibitory post-synaptic currents (mIPSCs) and muscle currents evoked by an exogenous GABA agonist (muscimol) (Figure 1A–E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-E

claim: An mIPSC corresponds to the current evoked by the fusion of a single synaptic vesicle at a GABAergic NMJ
source: An mIPSC corresponds to the current evoked by the fusion of a single synaptic vesicle at a GABAergic NMJ and, consequently, measures the function of synaptic UNC-49 receptors.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about mIPSCs

claim: Muscimol activates all surface UNC-49 receptors (including non-synaptic receptors in the nerve cord and muscle cell bodies)
source: Muscimol activates all surface UNC-49 receptors (including non-synaptic receptors in the nerve cord and muscle cell bodies).
evidence: Based on the known pharmacological properties of muscimol

claim: The mIPSC and muscimol-evoked current defects of unc-49 mutants were rescued by a transgene expressing GFP-tagged UNC-49B receptor in body muscles
source: The mIPSC (Figure 1A–C) and muscimol-evoked current (Figure 1D,E) defects of unc-49 mutants were rescued by a transgene expressing GFP-tagged UNC-49B receptor in body muscles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-E

claim: Muscimol-evoked currents were significantly larger in GFP-UNC-49B transgenic animals
source: Muscimol-evoked currents were significantly larger in GFP-UNC-49B transgenic animals (Figure 1E), presumably because this transgene is expressed at higher levels than the endogenous unc-49 gene.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The GFP-tag inserted into the TM3-4 loop did not impair UNC-49B receptor function
source: These results demonstrate that the GFP-tag (inserted into the TM3-4 loop) did not impair UNC-49B receptor function.
evidence: Inferred from the rescue experiments showing functional recovery

claim: In wild type animals, GFP-UNC-49B fluorescence exhibits a punctate distribution where each punctum is closely apposed to GABAergic motor neuron nerve terminals
source: In wild type animals, GFP-UNC-49B fluorescence exhibits a punctate distribution where each punctum is closely apposed to GABAergic motor neuron nerve terminals (labelled with mCherry-tagged RAB-3) (Figure 1F), consistent with prior studies (Thompson-Peer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and citation to Thompson-Peer et al., 2012

claim: In wild type controls, 40% of UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was mobile in FRAP experiments
source: In wild type controls, 40% of UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was mobile in FRAP experiments, with recovery occurring several minutes after photobleaching (Figure 1G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G,H

claim: In wild type animals, 46% of pH-UNC-49B synaptic fluorescence recovered following photobleaching
source: In wild type animals, 46% of pH-UNC-49B synaptic fluorescence recovered following photobleaching (Figure 1I).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1I

claim: Similar mobile fractions were observed with the GFP and pHluorin tagged receptors, suggesting that the majority of UNC-49B puncta fluorescence results from receptors in the plasma membrane
source: Because similar mobile fractions were observed with the GFP and pHluorin tagged receptors, these results suggest that the majority of UNC-49B puncta fluorescence results from receptors in the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of GFP and pHluorin FRAP data

claim: UNC-49B synaptic puncta comprise a mixture of mobile (~40% total) and immobilized (~60% total) receptors on the cell surface
source: Collectively, these results suggest that UNC-49B synaptic puncta comprise a mixture of mobile (∼40% total) and immobilized (∼60% total) receptors on the cell surface.
evidence: Inferred from FRAP experimental data

claim: Prior studies utilizing both FRAP and single molecule tracking techniques reported similar proportions of mobile and immobilized receptors at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses in cultured mammalian neurons
source: Prior studies utilizing both FRAP and single molecule tracking techniques reported similar proportions of mobile and immobilized receptors at both excitatory and inhibitory synapses in cultured mammalian neurons (Jacob et al., 2005; Ashby et al., 2006; Heine et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jacob et al., 2005; Ashby et al., 2006; Heine et al., 2008

claim: FRM-3 binds the UNC-49B TM3-4 loop in yeast 2-hybrid assays
source: To identify ERM proteins that could play a role in UNC-49B targeting, we screened all C. elegans ERM proteins and found that FRM-3 binds the UNC-49B TM3-4 loop in yeast 2-hybrid assays (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A

claim: FRM-3 is a band 4.1 (EPB4.1) paralog
source: FRM-3 is a band 4.1 (EPB4.1) paralog.
evidence: Based on sequence homology and established knowledge

claim: A frm-3 promoter construct expressed GFP in body muscles
source: First, we showed that a frm-3 promoter construct expressed GFP in body muscles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), consistent with FRM-3 function in muscles.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: GFP-tagged FRM-3 expressed in body muscles formed puncta in the nerve cord that were co-localized with a post-synaptic marker for GABAergic NMJs (mCherry-tagged NLG-1/Neuroligin)
source: Second, we showed that GFP-tagged FRM-3 expressed in body muscles formed puncta in the nerve cord that were co-localized with a post-synaptic marker for GABAergic NMJs (mCherry-tagged NLG-1/Neuroligin) (Pearson's correlation R = 0.80 ± 0.028, p = 0.02, n = 8) (Figure 2B) (Maro et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and citations to Maro et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2015

claim: FLAG-tagged FRM-3 and GFP-UNC-49B co-immunoprecipitated from worm extracts, when both were expressed in body muscles
source: Third, we showed that FLAG-tagged FRM-3 and GFP-UNC-49B co-immunoprecipitated from worm extracts, when both were expressed in body muscles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: FRM-3 is localized to GABAergic synapses where it may directly bind UNC-49B receptors
source: Collectively, these results suggest that FRM-3 is localized to GABAergic synapses where it may directly bind UNC-49B receptors.
evidence: Inferred from co-localization and co-immunoprecipitation data

claim: In frm-3 mutants, UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was significantly reduced
source: In frm-3 mutants, UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was significantly reduced and this defect was rescued by transgenes restoring FRM-3 expression in body muscles but not by those expressed in GABAergic motor neurons (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D

claim: mIPSC rate was unaffected in frm-3 mutants
source: mIPSC rate was unaffected in frm-3 mutants, implying that pre-synaptic GABA release was not significantly altered (Figure 2E,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,G

claim: mIPSC amplitude was significantly reduced in frm-3 mutants
source: mIPSC amplitude was significantly reduced in frm-3 mutants (Figure 2E,F), consistent with decreased UNC-49 abundance at synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,F

claim: The frm-3 mIPSC amplitude defect was rescued by transgenes restoring FRM-3 expression in body muscles
source: The frm-3 mIPSC amplitude defect was rescued by transgenes restoring FRM-3 expression in body muscles (Figure 2E,F), implying that FRM-3 acts in muscles to promote the function of synaptic UNC-49 receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,F

claim: Muscimol-evoked currents were unaltered in frm-3 mutants
source: Muscimol-evoked currents were unaltered in frm-3 mutants (Figure 2H); consequently, the frm-3 mutant mIPSC defect is unlikely to result from decreased bulk expression and surface delivery of UNC-49 receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2H

claim: Muscle FRM-3 promotes the localization and function of synaptic UNC-49 receptors but is not required for the function or trafficking of non-synaptic UNC-49 receptors
source: Collectively, these results suggest that muscle FRM-3 promotes the localization and function of synaptic UNC-49 receptors but is not required for the function or trafficking of non-synaptic UNC-49 receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of synaptic and total receptor measurements

claim: CASK is a synaptic scaffolding protein that binds directly to EPB4.1
source: CASK is a synaptic scaffolding protein that binds directly to EPB4.1 (Biederer and Sudhof, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Biederer and Sudhof, 2001

claim: C. elegans has two predicted CASK isoforms (LIN-2A and B), both encoded by the lin-2 gene
source: C. elegans has two predicted CASK isoforms (LIN-2A and B), both encoded by the lin-2 gene (Hoskins et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoskins et al., 1996

claim: LIN-2A and B share the PDZ, SH3, and GK domains while only LIN-2A contains the CaMK homology domain
source: LIN-2A and B share the PDZ, SH3, and GK domains while only LIN-2A contains the CaMK homology domain (Hoskins et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoskins et al., 1996

claim: LIN-2A is required for targeting epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFRs) to the basolateral domain of epithelial cells
source: LIN-2A is required for targeting epidermal growth factor receptors (EGFRs) to the basolateral domain of epithelial cells (Simske et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to Simske et al., 1996

claim: LIN-2A/CASK interacted with FRM-3/EPB4.1 in yeast 2-hybrid assays
source: Like their mammalian counterparts (Biederer and Sudhof, 2001), LIN-2A/CASK interacted with FRM-3/EPB4.1 in yeast 2-hybrid assays (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and citation to Biederer and Sudhof, 2001

claim: A lin-2 promoter construct expressed GFP in body muscles
source: A lin-2 promoter construct expressed GFP in body muscles, indicating that LIN-2A may function in muscles (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A

claim: mCherry-tagged LIN-2A expressed in muscles formed puncta in the nerve cords and these LIN-2A puncta were co-localized with GFP-UNC-49B at NMJs
source: mCherry-tagged LIN-2A expressed in muscles formed puncta in the nerve cords and these LIN-2A puncta were co-localized with GFP-UNC-49B at NMJs, consistent with LIN-2A binding to FRM-3 at NMJs (Pearson's correlation R = 0.68 ± 0.057, p = 0.04, n = 5) (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B

claim: lin-2 mutants had decreased UNC-49B puncta fluorescence
source: Like frm-3 mutants, lin-2 mutants had decreased UNC-49B puncta fluorescence (Figure 3C,D) and decreased mIPSC amplitudes (Figure 3E,F), both implying that synaptic UNC-49 levels were decreased.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C,D,E,F

claim: mIPSC rates were unaltered in lin-2 mutants
source: mIPSC rates were unaltered in lin-2 mutants (Figure 3G), indicating that pre-synaptic GABA release was unaffected.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3G

claim: Muscimol-activated current was unaffected in lin-2 mutants
source: Muscimol-activated current was unaffected in lin-2 mutants (Figure 3H), indicating that the lin-2 puncta and mIPSC defects were not caused by decreased bulk expression or surface delivery of UNC-49 receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H

claim: The lin-2 puncta and mIPSC defects were rescued by transgenes restoring LIN-2A expression in body muscles but not by those expressed in GABAergic motor neurons
source: The lin-2 puncta and mIPSC defects were rescued by transgenes restoring LIN-2A expression in body muscles but not by those expressed in GABAergic motor neurons (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,F

claim: UNC-49B puncta fluorescence and mIPSC amplitudes in frm-3 lin-2 double mutants were not significantly different from those in either single mutant
source: Consistent with this idea, UNC-49B puncta fluorescence and mIPSC amplitudes in frm-3 lin-2 double mutants were not significantly different from those in either single mutant (Figure 3D,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,F

claim: LIN-2A/CASK and FRM-3/EPB4.1 function together in body muscles to localize UNC-49B at NMJs but are not required for the expression or function of non-synaptic UNC-49 receptors
source: Collectively, these results suggest that LIN-2A/CASK and FRM-3/EPB4.1 function together in body muscles to localize UNC-49B at NMJs but are not required for the expression or function of non-synaptic UNC-49 receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of genetic and functional data

claim: mIPSC amplitudes were unaltered in lin-7 and lin-10 mutants
source: We found that mIPSC amplitudes were unaltered in lin-7 and lin-10 mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C), indicating that this complex is not required for UNC-49 synaptic targeting.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C

claim: In both frm-3 and lin-2 mutants, GFP-UNC-49B FRAP was significantly increased
source: In both frm-3 (Figure 4A) and lin-2 (Figure 4B) mutants, GFP-UNC-49B FRAP was significantly increased (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B,C

claim: The frm-3 FRAP defect was rescued by transgenes restoring FRM-3 expression in body muscles
source: The frm-3 FRAP defect was rescued by transgenes restoring FRM-3 expression in body muscles (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C

claim: A similar increase in FRAP was observed for pH-UNC-49B receptors in frm-3 mutants
source: A similar increase in FRAP was observed for pH-UNC-49B receptors in frm-3 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: Using a single copy RFP-tagged UNC-49B transgene (krSi2), a similar increase in FRAP of RFP-UNC-49B was observed in frm-3 mutants
source: Using this single copy transgene, a similar increase in FRAP of RFP-UNC-49B was observed in frm-3 mutants (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C,D

claim: Increased FRAP suggests that synaptic UNC-49B receptors had increased ability to undergo exchange in the nerve cord, most likely due to increased diffusional mobility in the plasma membrane
source: Increased FRAP suggests that synaptic UNC-49B receptors had increased ability to undergo exchange in the nerve cord, most likely due to increased diffusional mobility in the plasma membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the FRAP measurements

claim: LIN-2A and FRM-3 function as a scaffold that stabilizes an immobile pool of UNC-49 receptors in the plasma membrane at post-synaptic elements
source: These results suggest that LIN-2A and FRM-3 function as a scaffold that stabilizes an immobile pool of UNC-49 receptors in the plasma membrane at post-synaptic elements.
evidence: Inferred from the FRAP and localization data

claim: An nlg-1 promoter construct expressed GFP in body muscles
source: First, an nlg-1 promoter construct expressed GFP in body muscles (Hunter et al., 2010), consistent with NLG-1 function in muscles.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hunter et al., 2010

claim: mCherry-tagged NLG-1 expressed in body muscles was co-localized with GFP-tagged UNC-49B receptors at NMJs
source: Second, mCherry-tagged NLG-1 expressed in body muscles was co-localized with GFP-tagged UNC-49B receptors at NMJs (Pearson's correlation R = 0.81 ± 0.02, p = 0.01, n = 8) (Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A

claim: GFP-UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was significantly reduced in nlg-1 mutants
source: Third, GFP-UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was significantly reduced in nlg-1 mutants (Figure 5B,C), consistent with a decrease in total synaptic receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,C

claim: FRAP of GFP-UNC-49B, pH-UNC-49B, and single copy RFP-UNC-49B were all significantly reduced in nlg-1 mutants
source: Fourth, FRAP of GFP-UNC-49B (Figure 5D,E), pH-UNC-49B (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B), and single copy RFP-UNC-49B (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C,D) were all significantly reduced in nlg-1 mutants, indicating that the residual synaptic UNC-49B receptors were largely immobile.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D,E and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A,B,C,D

claim: NLG-1 stabilizes a mobile pool of surface UNC-49B receptors at synapses
source: These results suggest that NLG-1 stabilizes a mobile pool of surface UNC-49B receptors at synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the FRAP and localization data

claim: The mIPSC rate was significantly reduced in nlg-1 mutants
source: The mIPSC rate was significantly reduced in nlg-1 mutants (Figure 5F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F,G

claim: The mean mIPSC amplitude was significantly reduced in nlg-1 mutants
source: The mean mIPSC amplitude (Figure 5H) was also significantly reduced, consistent with decreased abundance of synaptic UNC-49.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H

claim: The nlg-1 mIPSC rate and amplitude defects were both rescued by a transgene restoring NLG-1 expression in body muscles
source: The nlg-1 mIPSC rate and amplitude defects were both rescued by a transgene restoring NLG-1 expression in body muscles (Figure 5G,H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G,H

claim: The muscimol-evoked current was unaffected in nlg-1 mutants
source: The muscimol-evoked current was unaffected in nlg-1 mutants (Figure 5I), indicating that the nlg-1 puncta and mIPSC defects were not caused by decreased bulk expression or surface delivery of UNC-49 receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I

claim: NLG-1 stabilizes a mobile pool of UNC-49 receptors at synapses, and that this receptor pool contributes to post-synaptic currents
source: Collectively, these results suggest that NLG-1 stabilizes a mobile pool of UNC-49 receptors at synapses, and that this receptor pool contributes to post-synaptic currents.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of FRAP and electrophysiology data

claim: Two recent studies also showed that NLG-1 promotes UNC-49 targeting to synapses
source: These results are consistent with two recent studies, which also showed that NLG-1 promotes UNC-49 targeting to synapses (Maro et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Maro et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2015

claim: C. elegans expresses long (NRX-1α) and short (NRX-1β) Neurexin isoforms, both encoded by the nrx-1 gene
source: C. elegans expresses long (NRX-1α) and short (NRX-1β) Neurexin isoforms, both encoded by the nrx-1 gene.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of C. elegans genetics

claim: NLG-1 binds to the sixth LNS repeat of NRX-1
source: NLG-1 binds to the sixth LNS repeat of NRX-1 (Hu et al., 2012) and, consequently, could bind to both NRX-1α and β.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al., 2012

claim: Mean mIPSC amplitude was significantly increased in nrx-1 null mutants
source: Mean mIPSC amplitude was significantly increased in nrx-1 null mutants (Figure 6A,B), indicating an increased number of functional UNC-49 receptors at synapses.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: The mIPSC rate was unaltered in nrx-1 mutants
source: The mIPSC rate was unaltered in nrx-1 mutants (Figure 6C), suggesting that presynaptic GABA release occurs normally.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C

claim: The amplitude of muscimol-activated current was unaltered in nrx-1 mutants
source: The amplitude of muscimol-activated current was also unaltered in nrx-1 mutants (Figure 6D); consequently, the increased mIPSC amplitude was unlikely to be caused by increased bulk expression or surface delivery of UNC-49 receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D

claim: GFP-UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was unaltered in nrx-1 null mutants
source: GFP-UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was also unaltered in nrx-1 null mutants (Figure 6E), suggesting that the mIPSC amplitude increase was not caused by increased abundance of synaptic UNC-49B receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E

claim: FRAP of synaptic GFP-UNC-49B was significantly reduced in nrx-1 mutants
source: Although UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was unaltered, FRAP of synaptic GFP-UNC-49B was significantly reduced in nrx-1 mutants (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F,G

claim: The nrx-1 mutant defects in mIPSC amplitude and UNC-49B FRAP were both rescued by transgenes expressing NRX-1α in GABAergic motor neurons but not by those expressing NRX-1β
source: The nrx-1 mutant defects in mIPSC amplitude (Figure 6B) and UNC-49B FRAP (Figure 6G) were both rescued by transgenes expressing NRX-1α in GABAergic motor neurons but not by those expressing NRX-1β.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,G

claim: NRX-1α transgenes expressed in body muscles lacked rescuing activity
source: NRX-1α transgenes expressed in body muscles lacked rescuing activity (Figure 6B,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B,G

claim: The total number of synaptic UNC-49B receptors was unaltered in nrx-1 mutants; however, there was a shift in receptor mobility whereby the pool of immobilized synaptic UNC-49B was enlarged (resulting in increased mIPSC amplitude) while the mobile pool was diminished
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the total number of synaptic UNC-49B receptors was unaltered in nrx-1 mutants; however, there was a shift in receptor mobility whereby the pool of immobilized synaptic UNC-49B was enlarged (resulting in increased mIPSC amplitude) while the mobile pool was diminished.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of puncta fluorescence, FRAP, and mIPSC data

claim: Pre-synaptic NRX-1α inhibits the immobilization of mobile UNC-49B receptors at synapses
source: These results support the idea that pre-synaptic NRX-1α inhibits the immobilization of mobile UNC-49B receptors at synapses.
evidence: Inferred from the FRAP and mIPSC data in nrx-1 mutants

claim: The effect of nrx-1 mutations on mIPSC amplitude was eliminated in nrx-1; nlg-1 double mutants
source: We found that the effect of nrx-1 mutations on mIPSC amplitude was eliminated in nrx-1; nlg-1 double mutants (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: The nrx-1 mIPSC amplitude defect was not blocked in nrx-1; frm-3 double mutants
source: By contrast, the nrx-1 mIPSC amplitude defect was not blocked in nrx-1; frm-3 double mutants (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B

claim: Presynaptic NRX-1α inhibits diffusional trapping of NLG-1-stabilized UNC-49 receptors but has little effect on the mobility of FRM-3-associated receptors
source: These results suggest that presynaptic NRX-1α inhibits diffusional trapping of NLG-1-stabilized UNC-49 receptors but has little effect on the mobility of FRM-3-associated receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the double mutant analysis

claim: UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was significantly reduced in frm-3 nlg-1 double mutants compared to the corresponding single mutants
source: Consistent with this idea, UNC-49B puncta fluorescence was significantly reduced (Figure 5B,C) while GFP-UNC-49B FRAP was significantly increased (Figure 7A,B) in frm-3 nlg-1 double mutants compared to the corresponding single mutants.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B,C and Figure 7A,B

claim: In frm-3 nlg-1 double mutants, both the immobile pool of synaptic UNC-49B and mIPSCs were completely eliminated
source: In frm-3 nlg-1 double mutants, both the immobile pool of synaptic UNC-49B (Figure 7A,B) and mIPSCs (Figure 5F) were completely eliminated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A,B and Figure 5F

claim: mIPSC rate was dramatically reduced in frm-3 nlg-1 double mutants compared to either single mutant
source: As an alternative, we measured mIPSC rate and found that it was dramatically reduced in frm-3 nlg-1 double mutants compared to either single mutant (Figure 5G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G

claim: Muscimol-activated muscle current in frm-3 nlg-1 double mutants did not significantly differ from wild type controls
source: Muscimol-activated muscle current in frm-3 nlg-1 double mutants did not significantly differ from wild type controls (Figure 5I), suggesting that the puncta, FRAP, and mIPSC defects were not caused by decreased bulk expression or surface delivery of UNC-49 receptors.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5I

claim: FRM-3 and NLG-1 stabilized UNC-49B receptors represent two distinct pools of synaptic receptors, which together account for all synaptic UNC-49 receptors
source: These results support the idea that FRM-3 and NLG-1 stabilized UNC-49B receptors represent two distinct pools of synaptic receptors, which together account for all synaptic UNC-49 receptors.
evidence: Inferred from the double mutant analysis showing complete elimination of synaptic receptors

claim: The coefficient of variation (CV) of the mIPSC amplitudes was ~0.6-7 in wild type animals
source: The coefficient of variation (CV) of the mIPSC amplitudes was ∼0.6–7 in wild type animals (Figure 7C,D), which is similar to values reported for some mammalian CNS synapses (Bekkers et al., 1990; Hanse and Gustafsson, 2001).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D and citations to Bekkers et al., 1990; Hanse and Gustafsson, 2001

claim: CV was significantly reduced in frm-3 and nlg-1 mutants and was not significantly altered in lin-2 mutants
source: Contrary to this idea, CV was significantly reduced in frm-3 and nlg-1 mutants and was not significantly altered in lin-2 mutants (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D

claim: The frm-3 and nlg-1 mIPSC amplitude CV defects were rescued by transgenes that restore expression of the corresponding genes in body muscles
source: The frm-3 and nlg-1 mIPSC amplitude CV defects were rescued by transgenes that restore expression of the corresponding genes in body muscles (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D

claim: Mean mIPSC amplitude was increased in nrx-1 mutants and decreased in lin-2 mutants while CV was unaltered in both cases
source: Mean mIPSC amplitude was increased in nrx-1 mutants (Figure 6B) and decreased in lin-2 mutants (Figure 3F) while CV was unaltered in both cases (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, Figure 3F, and Figure 7C

claim: The FRM-3 and NLG-1 scaffolds increase the diversity of quantal responses, and that this effect cannot be explained by changes in synaptic UNC-49 levels nor by changes in mean mIPSC amplitude
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the FRM-3 and NLG-1 scaffolds increase the diversity of quantal responses, and that this effect cannot be explained by changes in synaptic UNC-49 levels nor by changes in mean mIPSC amplitude.
evidence: Inferred from the CV analysis across different mutants

claim: Immobilized UNC-49B is stabilized at synapses via binding to FRM-3/EPB4.1 and LIN-2A/CASK
source: Second, immobilized UNC-49B is stabilized at synapses via binding to FRM-3/EPB4.1 and LIN-2A/CASK.
evidence: Inferred from the combination of binding, localization, and FRAP data

claim: Mobile UNC-49B is stabilized at synapses by post-synaptic NLG-1/Neuroligin
source: Third, mobile UNC-49B is stabilized at synapses by post-synaptic NLG-1/Neuroligin.
evidence: Inferred from the FRAP and localization data

claim: Pre-synaptic NRX-1α/Neurexin inhibits the immobilization of NLG-1 stabilized UNC-49B
source: Fourth, pre-synaptic NRX-1α/Neurexin inhibits the immobilization of NLG-1 stabilized UNC-49B.
evidence: Inferred from the FRAP and double mutant analysis

claim: The FRM-3 and NLG-1 stabilized receptor pools both contribute to inhibitory synaptic transmission
source: Fifth, the FRM-3 and NLG-1 stabilized receptor pools both contribute to inhibitory synaptic transmission.
evidence: Inferred from the mIPSC measurements in single and double mutants

claim: Both scaffolds increase the variability of quantal responses
source: Sixth, both scaffolds increase the variability of quantal responses.
evidence: Inferred from the CV analysis

claim: All synaptic UNC-49 receptors can be explained by the FRM-3 and NLG-1 scaffolds
source: And seventh, all synaptic UNC-49 receptors can be explained by these two scaffolds.
evidence: Inferred from the complete elimination of synaptic receptors in double mutants

claim: The FRM-3/EPB4.1 and LIN-2A/CASK scaffold accounts for ~40% of synaptic receptors while the NLG-1 scaffold accounts for ~30% of synaptic UNC-49
source: The FRM-3/EPB4.1 and LIN-2A/CASK scaffold accounts for ∼40% of synaptic receptors while the NLG-1 scaffold accounts for ∼30% of synaptic UNC-49 (assessed by puncta fluorescence).
evidence: Inferred from the quantitative analysis of puncta fluorescence in mutants

claim: In double mutants lacking both pools, immobilized synaptic UNC-49 receptors and mIPSCs are eliminated
source: In double mutants lacking both pools, immobilized synaptic UNC-49 receptors and mIPSCs are eliminated.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from double mutant analysis
